---
title: "The method"
---

## Two channels, two halves of the band

A converged probe illuminates a specimen and a pixelated detector records the full
diffraction pattern at every scan position. What reaches the detector splits
naturally in two, and the split is where the method starts.

**Inside the bright-field disk**, the transmitted beam interferes with itself.
Weak-phase scattering shifts the intensity distribution across the disk in
proportion to the local phase *gradient*, which is what single-side-band
ptychography reads. That works beautifully at low and mid spatial frequencies —
each frequency is measured by a pair of overlapping beams, and the overlap is
large — but the overlap shrinks as the spatial frequency approaches twice the
convergence angle, and past it there is none. Transfer falls to zero.

**Outside the disk**, scattering is incoherent to good approximation, and a
dark-field detector segment sees an image that shifts with defocus and with the
segment's angle — a parallax. Correcting those shifts and summing recovers high
spatial frequencies well. But a dark-field segment carries almost no low-frequency
information: at low frequency the parallax shift is small and the signal is
dominated by thickness and composition rather than phase.

So each channel is strong exactly where the other is weak. Neither spans the band.

## Fusing them

The fusion is a Wiener combination in the Fourier domain. Writing $P(\mathbf{q})$
and $D(\mathbf{q})$ for the two channels' spectra and
$\mathrm{SSNR}_P, \mathrm{SSNR}_D$ for their spectral signal-to-noise ratios,

$$
F(\mathbf{q}) \;=\;
\frac{\mathrm{SSNR}_P(\mathbf{q})\, P(\mathbf{q})
    + \mathrm{SSNR}_D(\mathbf{q})\, D(\mathbf{q})}
     {\mathrm{SSNR}_P(\mathbf{q}) + \mathrm{SSNR}_D(\mathbf{q})}
$$

which is the minimum-variance linear estimator when the two channels' noise is
independent. Each frequency is taken from whichever channel measures it better,
with the crossover placed by the data rather than by a chosen cutoff. Where one
SSNR vanishes the sum reduces to the other channel; where both are finite the
result is better than either.

The SSNR estimates are what make this more than a heuristic blend, and they are
measured, not assumed: the scan is split into two interleaved half-sets in a
checkerboard, each is reconstructed independently, and their difference gives the
noise power while their mean gives the signal power, frequency by frequency. That
costs two reconstructions per channel instead of one, and it means the weights
adapt to dose, thickness and specimen without a parameter to tune.

## Sub-pixel accumulation

Tilt-corrected dark field shifts each azimuthal segment by its parallax shift and
accumulates. How that shift is applied matters at low dose, and there are two
options.

`shift_method="fourier"` zero-pads and applies a phase ramp. It is exact for
dense, band-limited signals.

`shift_method="drizzle"` (the default) treats each input pixel as a small square
drop, places it at the shifted position, and distributes its flux to the output
pixels it overlaps by area — the drizzle of Fruchter & Hook (2002), specialised to
pure translations on a regular grid. Because every weight is non-negative, the
result is non-negative for non-negative input, and flux is conserved exactly.

The difference shows up when the frames are sparse. At very low dose a segment
image is a handful of single electron counts, and Fourier shifting turns each
isolated count into a sinc: roughly 20% negative side-lobes, with energy spread
across the whole frame. Drizzle has no ringing to spread.

::: {.callout-note}
The paper's figures were produced with the Fourier path; drizzle came afterwards.
Both are available, and on dense high-dose data they agree closely — on amorphous
carbon the fused images correlate to 0.9992.
:::

## What this is not

The direct ptychography here is non-iterative. It is a single linear inversion of
the bright-field intensity, not a phase-retrieval loop, so it has no convergence
behaviour, no step size and no initialisation beyond the aberration estimate. That
is why it runs in under a second on a 96² scan. It also means it inherits the weak-
phase approximation: strong scatterers and thick specimens depart from it, and an
iterative multislice reconstruction will do better there.
